message.content:
For a long, straight wire carrying a steady current \(I\), the magnetic field at a perpendicular distance \(r\) from the wire is given by Ampère’s law:

\[
B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}
\]

where  
- \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{H/m}\) (the permeability of free space).

Plugging in the numbers:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B &= \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{H/m}) \times 2\,\text{A}}{2\pi \times 4\,\text{m}} \\
  &= \frac{8\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{T·m}}{8\pi\,\text{m}} \\
  &= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}
\end{aligned}
\]

**Result:** The magnetic field at a point 4 m from the wire is **\(1.0 \times 10^{-7}\) tesla** (or 0.1 µT).

**Direction:** According to the right‑hand rule, if you point your thumb along the direction of the current (into the page in this case), your fingers curl around the wire; the magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the wire. At the point 4 m away, the field points tangentially to the circle centered on the wire.
